g.text: The MLOps lifecycle — from a support ticket to a live prediction
Goal · Route “I was charged twice” to billing. Follow one model from labeled examples to a cloud response.
Release and serve · Read from right to left
ML engineers build the router. AI engineers can use its result to draft a policy-based reply for agent review.
Blue = model or software Purple = versions or checks Orange = evidence Green = usable result
01 · One support ticket, two AI tasks
One support ticket, two AI tasks
A customer writes “I was charged twice.” What should the help desk do next?
Ask the room • Which output can you check with a single label?
The destination queue has a correct label. A reply also needs factual and human review.
AI is the broad field. Machine learning (ML) learns patterns from examples. Generative AI produces new content.
Shared work · Tests, deployment, monitoring and user feedback
AI engineer · Build the reply assistant
Both roles build software. Their day-to-day work overlaps, and job titles vary by team.
Ask the room • Which problem sounds more interesting to you?
If you enjoy studying routing errors, try the ML path. If you enjoy designing a useful reply assistant, try the AI path.
ONE EXAMPLE OF HOW A TEAM SHARES THE WORK
Choose labels and a simple baseline.
Train on past tickets and inspect mistakes.
Deliver a versioned model and evaluation report.
Connect a language model to approved policy.
Design prompts, test replies, add human review.
Deliver an assistant with a tested fallback.
03 · Why classical machine learning still matters
Classical ML often fits labeled tables, counts and categories.
A small model can run on a CPU and handle many requests at low cost.
Why classical machine learning still matters
Start with the decision the product needs. A support queue comes from a short, fixed list.
Try it • Compare the rule and the classifier on the same unseen tickets.
Pick the simplest model that meets your targets for routing quality, response time and cost.
Fast to write and easy to explain.
Test the limits with a ticket like
Inspect which words push a ticket
Keep or restore a working version
Find errors and act on them
Machine learning operations (MLOps) helps a team reproduce, release and maintain a model used by real people.
Ask the room • Could another engineer recreate last Friday’s router?
They need the training data version, code, settings, dependencies and the exact model that was released.
05 · Five rules for checking training data
Five rules for checking training data
Run these checks on the ticket export before training. This dataset has one row per resolved ticket.
Ask the room • A ticket appears twice with different labels. Which check fires first?
Uniqueness catches the repeated ID. Investigate the label conflict with the ticket owner before choosing a row.
Ticket ID, message and final queue are present.
Hold rows with a missing field.
Final queue is billing, account or delivery.
Each ticket ID appears once in this export.
Resolution time is at or after creation time.
The daily export arrives by the agreed cutoff.
Alert the owner and hold training.
06 · How the router learns and predicts
How the router learns and predicts
Training fits a model using known outcomes. Inference uses the saved model to predict a queue for a new ticket.
Check for leakage • Could we use the agent’s closing note as an input?
No. The closing note arrives after routing time. Use only information available when a new ticket arrives.
INFERENCE / WHEN A NEW TICKET ARRIVES
Fit on older tickets, tune on a later validation set, then test once on untouched newer tickets.
Baseline · Always choose “other” and score 90% accuracy, yet catch 0 of 10 billing tickets.
Worked example with 100 unseen tickets. A support agent confirms that 10 are billing tickets.
Ask the room • If missing a billing ticket is costly, which measure deserves attention?
Watch recall. Lowering the billing threshold may catch more tickets and send more false alarms to the billing team.
Of 10 actual billing tickets, 8 were caught.
08 · DVC and MLflow remember different parts of a run
DVC and MLflow remember different parts of a run
Suppose model v1 routed tickets well. How could a teammate reproduce it next month?
Model v1 → MLflow run → Git commit → DVC data version → the exact ticket export used for training.
Record the DVC data reference, Git commit, settings, evaluation scores and fitted pipeline with the run.
Keep the working router available while a candidate earns its way into production.
Continuous integration (CI) tests changes. Continuous delivery (CD) prepares approved releases.
Continuous training (CT) fits a new candidate on a trigger. Release checks still apply.
FROM A CHANGE TO A LIVE MODEL
Compare with v1 on the same held-out tickets.
Check billing recall, slow responses and queue errors.
Record the candidate and results in the model registry.
10 · Wrap the fitted model in a FastAPI service
Load the approved word-features + classifier pipeline once per server process. Keep its version with it.
Wrap the fitted model in a FastAPI service
An API gives another program a way to send a ticket and get a prediction using HTTP.
What happens if the request has no text field?
FastAPI validates the request against the schema and returns a validation error. The model never sees that request.
Python route · @app.post("/predict") → pipeline.predict([ticket.text]) → return queue and model version
11 · Put the model online and try one prediction
Routes a request to the service
Put the model online and try one prediction
A cloud service runs the API on a remote computer. The prediction can work while the developer’s laptop is off.
Demo in a deployed service · Open its /docs page, choose POST /predict, then Try it out and Execute.
Send a ticket. Look for HTTP 200, its predicted queue and the expected model version. The response below is an example.
WHEN A USER SENDS A TICKET
A region is a hosting location. Access rules control callers. Logs and metrics show errors, traffic and response times.
12 · What if the router starts making mistakes?
What if the router starts making mistakes?
A new “wallet top-up” issue appears. The service still responds quickly, but agents move more tickets to billing.
Ask the room • Should a change in vocabulary trigger an immediate release?
Verify the labels. Fix a broken input or test a new candidate, then run the release checks.
13 · How an AI engineer ships a reply assistant
How an AI engineer ships a reply assistant
The router predicts billing. Now the agent needs a draft that accurately reflects the current refund policy.
Try it • A draft promises an immediate refund, but its source only describes a review. What should happen?
Hold the draft. Save this as a test case for the next change to the prompt, model or policy.
This is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). If the policy is missing or unclear, hand the ticket to a person.
Learn basic Python, SQL and Git.
Load a CSV and write one test.
Train and evaluate a ticket router.
Use a small public or synthetic ticket dataset. Pick one path and show that someone else can run and evaluate your work.
What to show in a five-minute demo
Run one ticket end to end, show a failure you found, explain the fix and show the test that would catch it again.
For either project, add run instructions, log outcomes and document one limitation.

g.text: START HERE · 01 · Become an ML engineer
04 · Turn raw data into useful features
Learn to make a prediction, measure its errors and serve it in an application.
Learn Python, Git and SQL. Read a CSV, clean text,
and join each ticket to its final support queue.
Use vectors for features, probability for uncertainty,
and averages and distributions to describe data.
Try a keyword rule, then fit a linear classifier.
Keep newer tickets aside to test generalization.
Build a confusion matrix. Calculate billing recall.
Read missed tickets and write down why they failed.
Serve one model with FastAPI. Version the inputs,
track runs and monitor corrections after release.
First project · Route support tickets to billing or another team.
A support ticket is a recorded request for help, such as “I was charged twice.”
Build a product around a model. Learn to check whether its answers help a real user.
Learn Python, HTTP, JSON and tests. Send one
request to a model API and inspect the response.
Explore tokens, embeddings, context length and
next-token prediction. Trace a short prompt.
Retrieve an approved refund policy. Give the model
the policy and the ticket when asking for a draft.
Create example questions and expected facts.
Check citations, unsupported claims, cost and delay.
Start with agent approval. Log failures and turn
bad answers into cases for the next evaluation.
First project · A reply assistant that cites a policy passage.
Show one good reply and one case where your assistant asks a person for help.
Start with the output you need. Compare candidates against a simple baseline.
Predict a category. Use logistic regression on ticket
word counts. Compare with a decision tree.
Predict a number, such as resolution time. Start with
linear regression, then compare a boosted tree.
Random forests average trees. Gradient boosting
adds trees to correct earlier prediction errors.
Without queue labels, group similar ticket vectors
using k-means. Inspect examples from each group.
Use validation data to tune settings. Check recall
for routing and mean absolute error for time.
Practice · Compare two models on the same split.
Record the baseline, score, training time and three examples where each model fails.
Turn raw data into useful features
A feature is an input the model can use when it makes a prediction.
Ticket text, channel and creation time are available
when a customer first asks for help.
Use word counts or TF-IDF for text. One-hot encode
channel. Extract weekday from the timestamp.
Impute numeric values from the training set.
Use a safe fallback for unseen categories.
Split first. Fit vocabulary, imputation and scaling
only on training data. Exclude the final queue.
Use the same fitted transformations for validation,
testing and live requests. Save them with the model.
Practice · Does adding the channel improve billing recall?
Compare with the text-only baseline. Keep the feature only if it helps on validation data.
A neural network learns useful representations by adjusting weights to reduce a loss.
Practice shapes, matrix multiplication and activations.
Build a tiny network in PyTorch.
Send one batch through the network. Compare its
predictions with known labels using a loss function.
Compute gradients. An optimizer adjusts the weights.
Track training and validation loss. Try early stopping
or regularization when validation loss worsens.
Fine-tune a small pretrained text model. Compare its
recall, speed and cost with the classical baseline.
Practice · Train a small neural ticket classifier.
Next, study how a Transformer represents context and how a GPU speeds up tensor work.
Follow a decoder-only language model as it generates a draft reply, one token at a time.
Split the input into tokens. Map token IDs to vectors.
Position information tells the model their order.
Each query scores earlier keys and its own key.
The weights mix values across multiple heads.
Each position passes through a small neural network.
Residual paths and normalization connect the layers.
Stack attention and feed-forward blocks. Later
Project to vocabulary scores. Softmax gives
probabilities. Pick a token, append it and repeat.
Another design · The original Transformer has an encoder and a decoder.
The encoder reads the input. The decoder uses cross-attention to that input.
CUDA runs parallel calculations on NVIDIA GPUs. Tensor operations are one example.
Tokenize a batch of tickets on the host. Assemble
Move the model and inputs to GPU memory.
In PyTorch, select a CUDA device for both.
The framework calls GPU functions through CUDA.
Many threads compute pieces of a matrix operation.
Training also computes gradients to update weights.
Inference uses the fitted weights to predict.
Compare CPU and GPU time on the same batch.
Include transfer time and check peak GPU memory.
Practice · Compare one ticket with a batch of 128.
A classical ticket router can run on a CPU. A hosted model API handles the hardware for you.
